name: BlazingMQ
listed_description: Open source distributed message queuing system in C++ from Bloomberg with durable, fault-tolerant, highly performant queues and C++, Java and Python clients. (claim words: Book calls it highly performant and highly available; no numbers.; licence tag: Apache-2.0 (per repo page); book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 14, Understanding SOA, Message brokers)
reason: No measured comparison against RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka or ActiveMQ anywhere reachable. The repo README (https://github.com/bloomberg/blazingmq) only says high-performance, with no numbers; the repo docs/ folder holds only assets and mainpage.dox. The project docs site (bloomberg.github.io) does not resolve from this environment (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so I read its sources on the gh-pages branch via raw.githubusercontent.com. docs/performance/benchmarks.md has absolute BlazingMQ numbers only (6-node cluster with 1.5 ms ping, e.g. priority routing 1Q,1P,1C 60,000 msgs/s at p50 4.5 ms and p99 19.8 ms; 3-node low-ping setup p50 1.5 ms; broadcast 1Q,1P,5C 110,000 produce / 550,000 consume msgs/s) with no baseline system, no CPU model and no compiler flags. docs/introduction/comparison.md is a qualitative feature comparison against RabbitMQ and Kafka; its only RabbitMQ number is an architectural estimate (messages are stored once regardless of fan-out, so queues with fan-out ratio 50+ give 'storage savings of 50x when compared to RabbitMQ'), which is storage arithmetic, not a speed benchmark, and its other number is a bare 'median latency of ~5ms or less' with no baseline. Issues and PR titles mention Perf changes and unit benchmarks but no cross-system numbers. Search results found no third-party BlazingMQ vs Kafka/RabbitMQ benchmark. Directional claim plus absolute numbers only, so no record. Repo active (latest commit seen 2026-10-23), Apache-2.0.

name: Citus
listed_description: PostgreSQL extension for sharding, recommended because sharding can bring great performance at scale. (claim words: Book: sharding 'can often bring you great performance at scale'; recommends Citus for Postgres.; licence tag: None; book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 4, 'Replication patterns' (EPUB, no page numbers))
reason: No numeric comparison against single-node PostgreSQL on any page I could open. Opened: the repo README (adjectives only: high performance at any scale, fast analytical queries; its only number is a link slug 'making-postgres-stored-procedures-9x-faster-in-citus', whose baseline is Citus without stored-procedure delegation, not single-node Postgres), CHANGELOG.md (no speedup ratios), citus_docs performance_tuning.rst (absolute pgbench ingest rates on Citus Cloud, no single-node baseline), and https://github.com/citusdata/citus-benchmark (GPL-3.0 HammerDB TPROC-C and CH-benCHmark driver with a --no-citus flag to run plain Postgres, but no results, hardware or numbers published). Numbers that probably qualify exist only in pages blocked here (citusdata.com, docs.citusdata.com, dl.acm.org, learn.microsoft.com, devblogs.microsoft.com, techcommunity.microsoft.com, scribd all fail with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND): the SIGMOD 2021 industry paper 'Citus: Distributed PostgreSQL for Data-Intensive Applications' (Cubukcu et al., DOI 10.1145/3448016.3457551) says it reports benchmarks for four workload patterns, and WebSearch result text (not an opened page, source page not identified) quotes 'a benchmark SQL query running ~40x faster with an 8-node Citus cluster vs. a single Postgres node', Azure VMs with 16 vCPUs, 64 GB memory, network-attached disks with 7500 IOPS, Postgres 13, Citus 9.5, default settings, plus a Citus page advertising ~20X faster transactions against single-node Postgres, and a 2020 talk with >250x on GitHub-archive analytics. The 2023 GigaOM HammerDB study compares Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL (Citus) with CockroachDB and Yugabyte, not single-node Postgres. Not recorded because I could not open the source of any of these numbers. Worth a retry from an environment that reaches citusdata.com or the ACM paper: likely tier B (paper) or C (vendor), baseline single-node PostgreSQL, metric throughput or latency, hardware Azure 16 vCPU VMs, with the caveat that the gain depends on distributing tables on a shard key and on workloads that parallelise (a vendor-chosen multi-node cluster against one node).

name: librdkafka
listed_description: C/C++ client library for Apache Kafka; the book's modern-cpp-kafka and cppkafka examples depend on or wrap it. (claim words: Book only lists it as a Kafka client. Repo README claims over 1 million msgs/s producer and 3 million msgs/s consumer, with no hardware stated.; licence tag: BSD-2-Clause (per repo page); book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 15, Apache Kafka)
reason: The only numbers are the README claim 'current figures exceed 1 million msgs/second for the producer and 3 million msgs/second for the consumer', with no baseline, hardware, broker setup or message size. INTRODUCTION.md (read for 'throughput', 'benchmark', 'Java', 'faster') has tuning advice (batching, linger.ms) and behavioural notes against the Java client, with no measurements against it. The wiki titles (24 visible of 33) have no benchmark page. READMEs of confluent-kafka-python, confluent-kafka-go, confluent-kafka-dotnet, node-rdkafka, rdkafka-ruby and franz-go carry no benchmark comparison; rust-rdkafka's README (https://github.com/fede1024/rust-rdkafka) reports absolute BaseProducer numbers (1,045,413 messages/s at 10 byte messages, 24,623 messages/s at 10 KB) with no comparison client, and points to the kafka-benchmark tool. The third-party client comparisons I know of (Confluent blog benchmarks of the Python client, franz-go write-ups) are on blocked hosts and, for franz-go, use librdkafka as the baseline rather than the winner. Absolute claim without a named baseline, so no record. Repo BSD-2-Clause, active.

name: Memcached
listed_description: In-memory key-value cache used for cache-aside caching; book says such caches can be really fast and efficient, and notes it does not persist data. (claim words: Book: cache-aside caching with Memcached, Valkey or Redis 'can be really fast and efficient'; no numbers.; licence tag: None; book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 14, Outsourcing memory management, Which in-memory cache is better? | book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 4, 'Cache-aside cache' and 'Which NoSQL technology should I use?' (EPUB, no page numbers))
reason: No measured comparison against Redis or against direct database reads on any page I could reach. Read: repo README (adjectives only), the wiki Performance page (https://github.com/memcached/memcached/wiki/Performance, absolute 'can easily handle 200,000+ requests per second' and 'less than a millisecond on a good day', no baseline or hardware), and the docs site sources in https://github.com/memcached/memcached.github.io (content/_index.md: 'High end servers can serve millions of keys per second', no baseline; content/userguide/faq.md: memcached's ephemeral design lets it be '10x, 100x, or even 1000x faster than a traditional database', a rhetorical statement with no workload, hardware, named database or measurement; flashstorage, proxy, serverguide pages have no Redis or database comparison). https://github.com/memcached/mc-crusher is a load tool whose README has no results. Release notes compare memcached against its own earlier versions, not the listed baselines. Third-party Redis-vs-memcached numbers (vendor blogs, Dragonfly/KeyDB write-ups, the Facebook 'Scaling Memcache' paper) are on hosts blocked here or not on GitHub, and I used my search budget on other projects. Directional claim only, so no record. License is BSD-3-Clause per repo page (other bundled licences exist), active.
